sections.title: Mental model — what really happens when you run code

blocks.md: Picture the computer as a **very fast rule-follower**. It never guesses, never gets bored, and never does anything except what your recipe says. Your program is that recipe, written in C++. A program called the **compiler** translates your recipe into instructions the machine obeys, one by one.
**A variable is a labeled box in memory.** The label is the name you chose; inside sits exactly one value.

steps: You type instructions in C++ (the recipe)
Compiler translates recipe into machine instructions
CPU walks through instructions top to bottom
Boxes get filled, changed, read — screen shows results

blocks.md: **Golden rule:** the computer does *exactly* what you wrote — not what you *meant*. When output surprises you, re-read your lines like the rule-follower would.

items.q: You write `int count = 0` then later `count = 5`. What happened to the old 0?
options: It was replaced — the box now holds 5
items.explain: One box per name. Assigning overwrites whatever was inside.

options: To translate your text into machine instructions
items.explain: Translation first, execution after. Logic mistakes still pass through — the compiler only catches grammar-level errors.

blocks.md: Different contents need different boxes. `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds decimals, `char` holds ONE letter/symbol in single quotes, `bool` holds true/false, `string` holds text in double quotes.

blocks.label: boxes in action
blocks.py:
age = 21            # whole number box
price = 49.99       # decimal box
grade = 'A'         # ONE character (no separate char type)
passed = True       # yes/no box
name = 'Dhruv'      # text

print(name, 'scored', grade)

blocks.label: cin reads what user types
blocks.py:
n = int(input('Enter a number: '))
print('You typed', n)

items: `+ - * /` behave as expected on real numbers
`7 / 2` gives **3** — two whole-number boxes → decimal thrown away
`%` (modulus) keeps the leftover: `7 % 2` → **1**. It answers *"what remains after removing full groups"*

blocks.md: **Misconception alert:** `=` puts a value IN. `==` ASKS are they equal. Mixing them is the classic beginner bug.

blocks.label: which is largest?
blocks.py:
a, b, c = 12, 45, 30
print(max(a, b, c))          # builtin, but the if/else chain idea is the lesson

blocks.md: **A loop repeats work so you don't.** Three moving parts: start (`i=1`), keep-going test (`i<=n`), step (`i++`).

blocks.label: anatomy of for

blocks.md: **Trace tables are your superpower.** Machines follow steps blindly; tracing teaches YOU to be the machine. Every hard bug becomes findable.

items.explain: 3 goes into 10 three times (9 used), remainder 1.

items.q: How many times does `for(int i=0; i<4; i++)` run its body?
items.explain: i takes 0,1,2,3 — four passes. Off-by-one thinking starts here.
Left to right: 9/4=2 (whole), then 2*4=8. Order matters!

blocks.md: **A function does one job, takes the materials it needs, and hands back the answer.**
Inputs are called **parameters**, the handed-back result is the **return value**. Think vending machine: coins in (arguments), snack out (return).

blocks.label: one-job function
blocks.py:
def add_two(x, y):           # def = function; no return-type annotation needed
    return x + y

total = add_two(3, 4)
print(total)                  # 7

blocks.title: Trace: what travels when calling addTwo(3, 4)

blocks.md: This copying behavior is called **pass-by-value**: the function gets photocopies. Tearing the copy doesn't hurt your original document — changing `x` doesn't change the caller's variable.

items.q: After `void f(int a){ a=99; } int m=1; f(m);` — what is m?
items.explain: f got a COPY named a. Changing the copy never touches m.
void = 'no answer comes back'. It just DOES its job.

blocks.md: **A class is the blueprint; an object is the building made from it.** One blueprint, many buildings — each with its own paint and furniture.

blocks.label: blueprint + two buildings
blocks.py:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, roll):   # constructor; self = this object
        self.name = name              # members born by assignment
        self.roll = roll
    def introduce(self):
        print('I am', self.name, 'roll', self.roll)

s1 = Student('Asha', 1); s1.introduce()
s2 = Student('Bilal', 2); s2.introduce()

items: **object** = one actual thing built from it
**member** = a piece of data belonging to the object (`name`, `roll`)
**method** = an action the object can perform (`introduce()`)

items.q: `s1` and `s2` above — do they share the same `name` box?
options: No — each object owns its own members
items.explain: Each building has its own furniture. Sharing is special (that's `static`, met later).

blocks.md: A prime number can't be split into equal whole groups (except groups of 1 or itself). Test: try dividing by every number from 2 up to just below it. If any divides cleanly → NOT prime. Smaller numbers finish checking much sooner than big ones — remember that feeling; it becomes important later.

blocks.label: prime check

blocks.md: Every star pattern is just **rows × columns with a formula** connecting them. Three questions unlock ANY pattern: (1) How many rows? → outer loop limit. (2) Per row, what repeats? → inner loop. (3) How does column count relate to row number? → the formula.

steps: Row count → outer loop: r = 1 … n
Observe row 1: 1 star · row 2: 2 stars · row r: r stars
Formula: print stars while col ≤ r
Translate formula into inner loop: col = 1 … r

blocks.label: right triangle via formula

blocks.md: Hollow rectangle? Same skeleton — print star only when on an edge (`r==1 || r==n || c==1 || c==n`), space otherwise. Formula thinking replaces memorizing 20 patterns.

items.q: For an upside-down triangle (row 1 has n stars, shrinking), the inner loop formula is…
items.explain: row1→n stars, row2→n−1 … so stars = n − r + 1. Derivation beats memorization.

items.q: Why does isPrime stop early with return false?
options: One clean divisor proves NOT prime — more checking is wasted work
items.explain: First counterexample ends the debate. Early exits save steps.

sections.title: Step counting — your first complexity lens

blocks.md: Programs differ in **how many steps** they take. Counting steps tells you which solution finishes sooner. No symbols needed yet — just honest counting.
Nested loops multiply. That's why pattern printing feels heavy for big N — and why smarter tools (coming in later levels) hunt for ways to avoid nesting.
**More input usually means more steps — your job is knowing HOW MUCH more.**

sections.title: Problem set — L1 drills (one skill each)

items.title: Max of Three Numbers
items.statement: Read three integers, print the largest using ONLY if/else chains.
hints: Compare a against BOTH others with &&.
Chain: check a, else-check b, else it must be c.

solutionCode.label: if / else-if chain
solutionCode.py:
def max_of_three(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    if a >= b and a >= c:      # a beats BOTH others
        return a
    elif b >= c:               # a lost, so it is b vs c
        return b
    else:
        return c

items.complexity: Time O(1) — two comparisons at most. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why `>=` rather than `>`?
followups.a: With `>`, all-equal input (5,5,5) fails every branch in a chain written with strict comparisons and can fall through to a wrong result. `>=` makes ties resolve to the first candidate, which is correct since the values are equal anyway.

followups.q: Does the second branch need to re-check against a?
followups.a: No. Reaching the `else if` already proves a is not the maximum, so only b and c remain. Re-testing a would be dead logic — this is the whole point of an else-if chain over three independent ifs.

items.title: Triangle Validity
items.statement: Given three sides, decide if a triangle can exist (every pair's sum must beat the third side).
hints: Three checks needed: a+b>c AND a+c>b AND b+c>a.
Join them all with && in one if.

solutionCode.label: triangle inequality on all three pairs
solutionCode.py:
def is_triangle(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> bool:
    if a <= 0 or b <= 0 or c <= 0:      # degenerate sides
        return False
    return a + b > c and a + c > b and b + c > a

followups.q: Why are all three checks needed — is one not enough?
followups.a: Only if you already know which side is longest. Take (1,2,10): 2+10>1 and 1+10>2 both pass, yet it is not a triangle because 1+2 is not > 10. Checking all three pairs avoids having to sort first.

followups.q: Why strictly greater rather than ≥?
followups.a: Equality gives a degenerate triangle — the three points are collinear and the area is zero. (1,2,3) forms a straight line, not a triangle, so `>` is the correct boundary.

items.title: Factorial with a Loop
items.statement: Compute n! (product 1×2×…×n) iteratively. Trace n=5 on paper first!
hints: Start result at 1 (multiplying by 1 changes nothing).
Multiply result by every i from 2..n.

solutionCode.label: accumulate from 1

followups.q: Why start the loop at 2 instead of 1?
followups.a: Multiplying by 1 is a no-op, so starting at 2 saves an iteration. More importantly it makes 0! and 1! correct for free — the loop body never runs and the seed value 1 is returned.

followups.q: How large can n get before this breaks?
followups.a: 20! ≈ 2.4×10^18 is the last value that fits in a signed 64-bit integer; 21! overflows silently in C++. Python integers are arbitrary precision so they keep going — which is exactly why F013 exists as a C++ exercise.

items.title: Reverse a Number
items.statement: 1234 → 4321. Peel last digit with %, build the reversed number, shrink with /.
hints: rev = rev*10 + n%10 moves digits across.
n /= 10 chops the last digit off.
Loop until n becomes 0.

solutionCode.label: peel with %, rebuild with *10
solutionCode.py:
def reverse_number(n: int) -> int:
    negative = n < 0
    n = abs(n)
    rev = 0
    while n > 0:
        rev = rev * 10 + n % 10    # shift left, append last digit
        n //= 10                   # chop the digit we just used
    return -rev if negative else rev

items.complexity: Time O(number of digits) = O(log n). Space O(1).

followups.q: What does `rev * 10 + n % 10` actually do?
followups.a: Multiplying by 10 shifts every existing digit one place left, opening a units slot; `n % 10` reads the current last digit of the input and drops it into that slot. Repeated, it pours the digits out of one number and into the other in reverse order.

followups.q: LeetCode 7 requires returning 0 on overflow. How do you detect it?
followups.a: Before `rev = rev * 10 + d`, check whether rev already exceeds INT_MAX/10 — if so the multiplication will overflow. Handle the boundary case where rev == INT_MAX/10 by comparing d against the last digit of INT_MAX. Never let the overflow happen and then test for it; signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++.

items.title: Palindrome Number
items.statement: Check if the number reads the same backwards (121 ✓, 123 ✗). Reuse your reverse trick.
hints: Reverse into a second variable.
Compare original with reversed using ==.

solutionCode.label: reverse and compare
solutionCode.py:
def is_palindrome_number(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 0:                       # the minus sign never mirrors
        return False
    rev, copy = 0, n
    while copy > 0:
        rev = rev * 10 + copy % 10
        copy //= 10
    return rev == n

followups.q: Why are negative numbers excluded?
followups.a: Reversing -121 digit-wise gives 121-, which is not a number. By convention the problem treats no negative value as a palindrome, so returning false immediately is both correct and a useful early exit.

followups.q: Can you avoid reversing the whole number?
followups.a: Yes — reverse only the second half and compare it to the first. Stop when the remaining input is ≤ the reversed half. It halves the work and sidesteps overflow entirely, since the half-reversal never exceeds the original.

items.title: Sum of Digits
hints: sum += n % 10 collects each digit.
Then n /= 10 discards it.

solutionCode.label: same peel, accumulate instead of build
solutionCode.py:
def sum_of_digits(n: int) -> int:
    n = abs(n)
    total = 0
    while n > 0:
        total += n % 10         # collect the digit
        n //= 10                # discard it
    return total

followups.q: What does this return for n = 0?
followups.a: 0. The loop never runs and the seed is returned. That is the correct answer, but note it is the one input where the loop body executes zero times — a classic off-by-one spot if you write a do-while instead.

followups.q: What is a digital root and how does it relate?
followups.a: Repeatedly summing digits until one digit remains. There is a closed form: 1 + (n−1) mod 9 for n > 0. Interviewers use it to check whether you reach for a loop when arithmetic already answers it.

items.title: Solid & Hollow Rectangle
items.statement: Print an R×C rectangle twice: fully starred, then hollow (stars only on borders).
hints: Edge test: r==1 || r==R || c==1 || c==C.
Elsewhere print space. Keep both loops identical shape.

solutionCode.label: same loop shape, different cell test

items.complexity: Time O(R·C) — one visit per cell. Space O(R·C) for the returned string.

followups.q: Why is the border test an OR of four conditions rather than an AND?
followups.a: A cell is on the border if it is on ANY edge — first row, last row, first column, or last column. AND would demand all four simultaneously, which is only true for a 1×1 grid.

followups.q: What happens when R or C is 1 or 2?
followups.a: Every cell satisfies at least one edge condition, so the hollow rectangle is identical to the solid one. That is correct — there is no interior to hollow out — and it is the edge case worth stating before the interviewer asks.

items.title: Half & Full Pyramid
items.statement: Half pyramid (c ≤ r), then full pyramid (spaces formula + odd-star formula).
hints: Full pyramid spaces per row = n − r.
Stars per row = 2*r − 1 (odd numbers!).

solutionCode.label: half: c <= r. full: (n-r) spaces then 2r-1 stars

items.complexity: Time O(n²) — the number of characters emitted. Space O(n²) for the returned string.

followups.q: Where does 2r − 1 come from?
followups.a: A centred pyramid grows by one star on each side per row, so widths go 1, 3, 5, … — the odd numbers. Row r is the r-th odd number, which is 2r − 1. Deriving it beats memorising it, because the same reasoning gives 2r − 1 spaces for an inverted or diamond variant.

followups.q: Why does the space count use n − r?
followups.a: The pyramid must be centred in a field of width 2n − 1. Row r has 2r − 1 stars, leaving (2n − 1) − (2r − 1) = 2(n − r) spaces split evenly across both sides, so n − r on the left. Trailing spaces are usually omitted.

items.title: Prime Check
items.statement: Implement isPrime from this section and test 1, 2, 9, 17, 97.
hints: Handle n ≤ 1 FIRST to dodge wrong 'true'.
Any clean division ends with return false.

solutionCode.label: trial division up to the square root
solutionCode.py:
def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n <= 1:                    # 0, 1 and negatives are not prime
        return False
    if n <= 3:                    # 2 and 3 are
        return True
    if n % 2 == 0:                # no other even is
        return False
    i = 3
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:            # a clean division ends it
            return False
        i += 2
    return True

followups.q: Why is stopping at √n sufficient?
followups.a: If n = a×b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n. So any composite has a factor at or below its square root; finding none proves primality. Checking beyond √n only re-finds the mirrored partners of factors already tested.

followups.q: Why does n ≤ 1 have to be handled first?
followups.a: For n = 1 the loop body never executes, so the function would fall through to `return true` and declare 1 prime. Ordering the guard first is what makes that impossible — the classic bug this exercise is built to expose.

items.title: FizzBuzz
items.statement: 1..n: multiples of 3 → Fizz, of 5 → Buzz, both → FizzBuzz, else the number.
hints: Check 'both' case FIRST (divisible by 15).
Order of checks is everything here.

solutionCode.label: test the combined case first

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the returned list.

followups.q: What breaks if the %15 test comes last?
followups.a: 15 matches `i % 3 == 0` first and the chain emits "Fizz", never reaching the combined case. In an else-if chain the most specific condition must be tested first — that ordering is the entire point of the exercise.

followups.q: Why 15 rather than testing both %3 and %5?
followups.a: They are equivalent: 15 is lcm(3,5), so divisibility by 15 is exactly divisibility by both. Writing `i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0` is arguably clearer and generalises better when the divisors are not coprime — lcm, not the product, is the right constant.

revisionCard: Variable = labeled box; assignment REPLACES contents
Integer division drops decimals; % gives the remainder
for-loop = start · keep-going-test · step; trace tables catch bugs
Class = blueprint, object = building with its own members
Patterns = outer rows × inner cols joined by a FORMULA, not memory
